doc.title: Fred Radke interviewed by Monk Rowe, Hillsdale, Michigan, November 8, 2023

title: Joining San Francisco Local 6 and calling trumpet players weekly
summary: He rose to first chair, joined the union at 15 with teacher Dick Lawter's advice, and phoned the city's trumpet players weekly until a contractor called.

story.theme_name: The musicians' union: cards, locals, and the Black-white merger
story.community_name: The musicians' union: cards, scale and the black-white merger

blocks.x: morning ‘til nine at night, marching, doing routines, learning marches. I went from 67th chair to first chair, and later on became the assistant conductor of the band when I was about 14. And so then I left the band and of course I’m listening to Harry James all the time. I mean he’s my mentor. It’s all — that’s — focused on Harry. And so my teacher says, “You know if you’re going to play you should join the union.” So I joined the union when I was 15 and yes I auditioned. I had to play all my major scales and play “Stardust.”
Do you think they would have denied you membership if you couldn’t play that well? Because I’ve heard a couple of stories from other musicians —

Well it all depends where you were. This is San Francisco Local 6. So I don’t know. I mean later on I think everybody had to audition in those times, and it was I think $50 to join the union and $9 a quarter or something you know. So my teacher was the top trumpet player in San Francisco. Dick Lawter and a first call guy. And so see that’s the smart thing to do. If you move to a city, I’ve told students this, if you want to go to New York or something, or wherever, find out who the number one call player is, and you call him up and say, “Hi this is Fred Radke, I’m a trumpet player and I’m moving to New York because I want to study with you and no one else.” And naturally the guy will say, “Well I don’t teach anymore” or “I’m busy.” And you say, “Okay, well this is the reason I’m coming to the City, I want to meet you and I want to study with you.” So you let that rest for a few days, you call him back again, finally the guy says, “All right, why don’t you come by.” Boom — there you go. So Dick Lawter gave me a list of all the trumpet players in San Francisco, which there are really good trumpet players. And he says, “You call these guys every week.” So I remember — I had the union book and I listed out like ten or fifteen trumpet players. And you would get a call every Wednesday afternoon from Fred Radke. Well after you figure out it said, “Who in the heck is Fred Radke? Well he keeps calling me.” And this is strange — Saturday a lot of times you would get a call to make a gig Saturday night, like 4:00 — somebody would get sick, there was a contractor saying well I need a trumpet player. So one night I get a call at 5:30. They said, “This is Fred Radke? This is Jack Fisher” who was a big contractor in San Francisco. I’ve got a show and a dance tonight at the Fairmont Hotel, my trumpet player came down with the flu, I need somebody, you come highly recommended from Dick Lawter, so the talk-over is at 7:00, the show is at 8:30, we play from 10 to 1:00 — tuxedo and be there.” And I said, “Okay, what is the show?” All of a sudden for some reason I guess my voice, something says, “How old are you?” I said, “I just turned 16.” “Have you ever played a show?” I said, “No.” And he said, “Well then I can’t use you, I’m sorry, good luck to you.” And I said, “Wait a minute, I have a question for you.” I said, “How do you have an opportunity or experience to play a show if no one ever hires you because you haven’t played a show, so therefore how do you do that?
